prompt: Match each document to the question it answers.
hint: One of the questions on the right belongs to none of the four.

pairs.right: Where do we want to be?
How will we get there, given what is in the way?
What will we do, in what order?

prompt: Put the four documents in order, from the one that should change most often to the one that should change least.
hint: The further a document looks, the less often it should change.
trap: Placing the strategy last treats it as the most important document; the vision looks further ahead and changes more rarely still.

prompt: Helena's sentence reads: "A buyer at a 10:00 on-sale gets the same checkout as a buyer at three in the morning." What makes it a vision rather than a strategy?
hint: Which of the four questions does it answer?

choices.text: The CTO wrote it, and the vision belongs to the CTO
choices.why: Authorship follows from the kind of document; it does not define it. A CTO who writes a list of quarters has written a roadmap.

choices.text: It sets a target the teams can be measured against
choices.why: As written it has no number to measure, and a target with no approach is the goal that lesson 1 warned about.

choices.text: It says where to be, and names no obstacle and no way there
choices.why: Right: no technology, no date, no obstacle named. The strategy is the document that says how, given what is in the way.

choices.text: It is short enough to repeat in an all-hands meeting
choices.why: A one-line strategy policy is short too. Length does not decide which question a document answers.

prompt: A team's backlog has had the same items at the top for six months. What does the lesson read into that?
hint: How often should a backlog change?

choices.text: The team plans well, and its priorities are stable
choices.why: Stability is right for a vision. A backlog is the next few sprints, and one that does not move is not being worked from.

choices.text: It lists things nobody is doing; the work happens elsewhere
choices.why: Right: a backlog changes every sprint as work is finished and replaced. Six months unchanged means the work is happening somewhere else.

choices.text: The strategy above it has stopped changing, so the backlog has too
choices.why: The strategy is meant to change rarely. That gives the backlog no reason to freeze, because the backlog moves at its own pace.

choices.text: It has turned into a roadmap and should be redrawn by quarter
choices.why: A roadmap changes every quarter, so a list unchanged for two quarters is not behaving like one either.

prompt: By the lesson, who writes the roadmap?
hint: Lesson 18 is about writing it with two pens.

choices.text: Engineering, since it lists technical work
choices.why: A roadmap drawn up by engineering alone drifts into a list of engineering wishes in date order.

choices.text: The CTO, who also signs the strategy and owns the vision
choices.why: The CTO owns the vision and signs the strategy; the roadmap is where engineering and product plan together.

choices.text: Product and engineering, together
choices.why: Right: most of what engineering builds is product work, and the roadmap is the document other departments plan against.

choices.text: Each team, by merging the tops of their backlogs
choices.why: Merged backlogs give a list with no order between teams and no reason above it.

prompt: Which question does a strategy answer that a roadmap cannot?

choices.text: When will each project ship?
choices.why: Dates are the roadmap's job; it is the document with a calendar on it.

choices.text: How much will the year's engineering cost?
choices.why: Neither document is a budget; lesson 11 is about that one.

choices.text: Which team owns each piece of work?
choices.why: Ownership appears on a roadmap and in a strategy's actions alike, so it does not separate them.

choices.text: Why this, and not that?
choices.why: Right: the strategy carries the diagnosis and the policy, which is where the reason for choosing comes from.

prompt: Coreto's old roadmap could have delivered every quarter on time. Why would it still have been the wrong year?

choices.text: Its four projects were too large for one quarter each
choices.why: The question assumes they shipped on time; the size of the projects is not what was wrong.

choices.text: The failing on-sales, the problem that cost venues, were absent
choices.why: Right: a roadmap states no problem to check against, so the one that cost Coreto venues could be left out without anybody noticing.

choices.text: Product had not been asked, so the dates clashed with launches
choices.why: A roadmap with two authors is better, but a perfectly aligned one would still have left out the on-sales.

choices.text: It had no vision statement on the slide before it
choices.why: A vision on top would not have named the problem either; that is the strategy's diagnosis.

prompt: Platform's load test will take a month longer than planned. Which document should change?
hint: Which of the two absorbs a slipped date?

choices.text: The roadmap moves with the new date; the strategy stays
choices.why: Right: absorbing change cheaply is one of the things a roadmap is for. The diagnosis and the policy have not moved.

choices.text: The strategy, so that its actions carry the new date
choices.why: A strategy rewritten every time a date slips was never a strategy; it was the roadmap again.

choices.text: Both, because they have to stay in step with each other
choices.why: They stay consistent through the trace, not by being edited together; a date belongs to one of them.

choices.text: Neither: a date on a roadmap is a commitment and is held
choices.why: Holding a date that reality has moved is how a roadmap stops being believed. Lesson 11 of delivery-metrics is about honest dates.

prompt: The sharpest of the three checks: a strategy can explain why a project is ___ from the plan, and a roadmap on its own cannot.
hint: Ask why the front-end framework is not there.

prompt: Which of these does a roadmap do that a strategy does not? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of who plans against it, and what happens when a date slips.

choices.text: Puts the work in sequence and shows dependencies
choices.why: Right: the strategy says the load test comes first; the roadmap puts it in a quarter.

choices.text: Names a problem that somebody could check against data
choices.why: That is the strategy's diagnosis. A roadmap names deliverables.

choices.text: Gives sales, product and finance dates to plan against
choices.why: Right: other departments plan against the roadmap because it has dates and the strategy does not.

choices.text: Explains why a proposal is left out of the year
choices.why: Absence has no reason on a roadmap; the policy is what rules things out.

choices.text: Absorbs a slipped date without the strategy changing
choices.why: Right: the roadmap moves and the strategy stays, which is the right way round.

prompt: In the table of Coreto's Q2 roadmap lines, how many trace to nothing?
hint: Product work and keeping the lights on both count as a trace.

prompt: Platform's upgrade of Rails and Ruby to supported versions traces to no action in the strategy. What does the lesson say to do with it?
hint: Four kinds of answer in the column, and one problem.

choices.text: Stop it, since work that traces to no action is an orphan
choices.why: An orphan traces to nothing at all. Keeping the lights on is a trace, and the work is not optional.

choices.text: Link it to action 3, because the reservation module runs on Rails
choices.why: That is the invented link the lesson warns about; once every line claims the strategy, the claims mean nothing.

choices.text: Label it honestly as keeping the lights on
choices.why: Right: a framework past its supported life is real, required work, and the label says exactly what it is.

choices.text: Postpone it until a strategy covers maintenance
choices.why: The supported life ends on a date somebody else chose; waiting for a strategy to mention it does not move that date.

prompt: The deploy freeze was on the roadmap for Q3, and no team had the on-sale calendar in its backlog. What does the lesson call that?
hint: Which direction was the trace being followed in?

choices.text: An orphan
choices.why: An orphan is work with no reason above it. Here the reason exists and the work below it does not.

choices.text: Decoration: a commitment that no backlog reaches
choices.why: Right: tracing the action down stopped halfway, so it read as a commitment while the freeze depended on somebody remembering.

choices.text: Keeping the lights on, which needs no backlog item
choices.why: The freeze is action 4 of the strategy, not maintenance, and every kind of work needs somebody doing it.

choices.text: A roadmap standing in for the strategy
choices.why: Coreto has both documents and they agree; the gap is between the roadmap and the backlogs.

prompt: Trace this piece of Coreto's work upwards: put the four links in order, starting from the backlog.
items: Replay a past on-sale's traffic in the load test
Q1: on-sale load test in place
Action 2: build the load test before changing the code
The 10:00 buyer gets the same checkout as the 3 a.m. buyer
trap: Putting the action below the roadmap line reverses the direction of the reason: the roadmap line exists because the action does.

prompt: A Reservations change traces cleanly to action 3, but its design will make the seat-hold code harder to change. What does the trace tell you about it?
hint: Which single question does the trace answer?

choices.text: That it is approved, because it serves the strategy
choices.why: A clean trace says the work has a reason. Whether it is done well is a different question the column does not answer.

choices.text: That it is an orphan, because a bad design serves nothing
choices.why: An orphan traces to nothing; this one traces to action 3. Quality and reason are separate questions.

choices.text: That the trace column needs a quality rating beside it
choices.why: The lesson keeps the trace to one question on purpose; design is judged in review, and cost by the money of lessons 5 and 13.

choices.text: Nothing about its quality: only that the work has an agreed reason
choices.why: Right: the trace is silent on whether the work is done well, sized right or worth its cost.

prompt: A company's slide titled "Technical strategy 2027" shows: Q1 Kubernetes, Q2 observability, Q3 data platform, Q4 multi-region. Which document is it?
hint: Does it name a problem, or explain an absence?

choices.text: A strategy, since it covers a year of work
choices.why: Covering a year is not what makes a strategy; it has no diagnosis and could not say why anything is absent.

choices.text: A roadmap: projects by quarter, with no stated problem
choices.why: Right: it answers what and when. Ask why multi-region comes after the data platform and the slide has no answer.

choices.text: A vision, because it looks a year ahead
choices.why: A vision says where to be and names no technology; this names four technologies and four dates.

choices.text: A backlog that has been grouped into quarters for presentation
choices.why: A backlog is the next few sprints of one team; four quarter-long projects are roadmap lines.

prompt: Match each finding to the name the lesson gives it.
hint: Two of them come from tracing, in opposite directions.

pairs.left: A roadmap line that traces to nothing
A strategy action that no backlog item reaches
A strategy rewritten each time a date slips
A backlog unchanged for six months

prompt: Mobile's GraphQL gateway traces to nothing. Which outcome does the lesson rule out?

choices.text: The gateway carries on as before, with nobody examining it
choices.why: Right: an orphan has to be stopped, justified in the open or reclassified. Carrying on unexamined is the outcome ruled out.

choices.text: The work stops and the engineers move to work that traces
choices.why: Stopping is one of the three acceptable outcomes, and here the likeliest, since the policy ruled the migration out.

choices.text: The strategy is amended in the open to include it
choices.why: Amending the strategy in the open is acceptable: everybody sees the change and can argue with it.

choices.text: It is reclassified honestly as product work
choices.why: If it really is product work, saying so is acceptable; the word that matters is honestly.

prompt: A strategy action that reads as a commitment, with no backlog item anywhere below it, is what the lesson calls ___.
hint: It looks good on the wall.
